strengths: The paper addresses a relevant NLP evaluation problem: measuring changes in social bias after continued masked-language-model training. Comparing each retrained model with its pretrained base is well motivated.

The experiments cover four identified MLM checkpoints, two established benchmarks, several scoring baselines, and detailed category-level results. Retraining in both stereotypical and anti-stereotypical directions provides useful evidence of sensitivity to training exposure.
Equations and worked examples help explain the scoring procedures. CRR, ΔP, and ΔPA consistently recover the expected retraining direction across the 72 reported model/category/direction cases.
weaknesses: The central claim of more accurate bias measurement is insufficiently validated. Retraining uses an 80/20 split of CrowS-Pairs, while evaluation is reported over CrowS-Pairs without a separate test set. Results may therefore reflect memorization of training sentences. Moreover, the correct direction is assigned from the retraining corpus, rather than independently measured model behavior. The reported 100% accuracy establishes agreement with this assumed direction at the category level. Evaluation on disjoint sentence pairs and neutral retraining controls is needed before recommending Findings. Claims that other metrics underestimate or overestimate pretrained bias similarly lack an independent reference.

Human-annotation validation provides weak additional support (Section 3.4.2 and Appendix M). The best AUROCs are 0.572 versus AUL's 0.566 for RoBERTa, and 0.571 versus 0.569 for BERT. No confidence intervals or significance tests establish these small improvements, and there are only 58 negative pairs against 1,450 positive pairs. These annotations describe whether text expresses stereotypes and provide only indirect validation of model-specific bias. The statement that thresholds maximize AUROC also needs clarification.

BSRT has an unresolved interpretation problem: Equation 10 returns zero when two models are identical, yet Section 3.5.2 interprets scores below 50 as a shift toward the opposite bias direction. Ties therefore require explicit neutral handling, especially for discrete rank-based measures. Additionally, Appendix P's McNemar test assesses changes in binary sentence preferences; it does not directly test the preference-gap changes aggregated by BSRT. Direct uncertainty estimates for that statistic are missing.

The added value of the proposed attention weighting is not established. Existing CRR already achieves the reported 100% direction-classification accuracy. CRRA simultaneously introduces attention weighting and changes the rank transformation, so comparison with CRR does not isolate the contribution of attention. An unweighted log-rank control and evidence beyond the saturated classification result would clarify the supported methodological contribution.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite useful checkpoint names, masking probability, and epoch counts. The manuscript claims a package release but supplies no package or repository link. Optimizer settings, learning rate, batch size, random seeds, split construction, and precise attention aggregation are insufficiently specified. Variation across retraining runs is also unreported.

Some numerical reporting requires reconciliation. Table 3 presents per-model error rates in increments of approximately 1/36, although each model/direction has nine category predictions. For example, one incorrect category is reported as 0.028 rather than 1/9. Furthermore, Table 16 shows four wrong-direction AULA categories for BERT retrained on the anti-stereotypical set, while Table 3 reports 0.083. Explicit denominators, tie handling, and corrected counts are necessary to audit the headline comparison.
